Note: MDR-TB and rifampicin combinations are excluded from these fit metrics because all TB cases are modelled as rifampicin-resistant by definition, which would skew overall resistance metrics. Listeria monocytogenes is also excluded because its very low infection incidence yields unstable resistance percentages at simulation scale.
These fit metrics average over bacteria/drug combinations, whereas the microbiome benchmarks below describe the share of the total population carrying any resistant microbiome.

Footnotes

(1) Infection deaths target: 7.7 million deaths associated with 33 bacterial
    pathogens (GBD 2019; published 95% uncertainty interval 5.7-10.2 million).
    The published central estimate is used unchanged as a pragmatic benchmark for
    the model's 2025 output rather than applying a small, precision-implying scope
    adjustment. The simulation numerator counts person-level sepsis-related plus
    non-sepsis infection deaths with at least one contributing infection other than
    H. pylori or MDR-TB; concurrent excluded infections do not remove an otherwise
    in-scope death. The model organism set and taxonomic resolution differ slightly
    from the GBD 33-pathogen analysis, and the source estimate is for 2019. These
    differences are documented as interpretation limits. The target is not an
    estimate of deaths attributable to antimicrobial resistance.

(2) Antibiotic use target: 100 million people on antibiotics on an average day.
    This target was revised downward because Klein et al. (2018, PNAS 115:E3463-E3470)
    is fundamentally a consumption paper reporting DDDs from sales data, not a direct
    count of unique people on treatment on an average day. Treating DDD totals as daily
    users tends to overstate person-prevalence because prescribed daily doses vary by
    drug and syndrome, some regimens exceed 1 DDD/day, and sales volumes include leakage
    from wastage, stock buffering, and non-human channels. Browne et al. (2021, Lancet
    Planetary Health 5:e893-e904) estimated 14.3 DDDs per 1,000 inhabitants per day
    globally in 2018 (95% uncertainty interval 13.2-15.6), which implies roughly 117
    million DDD-equivalents/day at a world population of 8.2 billion. WHO describes
    DDDs per 1,000 inhabitants per day as only a rough proxy for people treated; unique
    daily users should sit below that DDD total in a person-based model. The
    revised 100 million target therefore treats antibiotic prevalence as a pragmatic
    person-day calibration benchmark rather than a literal transcription of DDD-based
    consumption. It is not a published unique-user estimate.

(3) Bacterial infection incidence target: 20% of the world population per year,
    with a derived plausible range of 15-30%. The 42 organism-specific targets sum
    to 22.34% after selectively updating E. coli, Shigella, and Campylobacter using
    the WHO FERG 2021 estimates (Majowicz et al. 2026, Lancet Global Health,
    doi:10.1016/j.langlo.2026.103997). That analysis estimated 426 million Shigella
    illnesses (95% uncertainty interval 234-711 million), 291 million Campylobacter
    illnesses (169-459 million), and 260 million ETEC illnesses (152-423 million).
    The E. coli target uses ETEC as a conservative source-informed floor, while the
    model category also includes other E. coli syndromes; the Campylobacter source
    category is broader than the model's C. jejuni category. The person-level headline
    counts at most one acquisition day per person, so 20% allows for same-day
    polymicrobial acquisitions present in the summed organism targets. This is a
    derived model-scope benchmark, not a published estimate of all bacterial infections.

(4) Sepsis target: 70 million incident cases per year (bacterial sepsis only),
    with a derived plausible range of 50-100 million. The GBD 2021 Global Sepsis
    Collaborators (2025, Lancet Global Health 13:e2013-e2026) estimated 166 million
    all-cause sepsis cases in 2021 (95% uncertainty interval 135-201 million). That
    estimate includes sepsis outside this bacteria-only model's scope, including
    viral, fungal, and parasitic sepsis and the wider burden of sepsis complicating
    non-infectious disease. The 70 million target and 50-100 million range are thus
    explicit model-scope assumptions informed by GBD, not a published GBD bacterial-
    sepsis point estimate or 95% uncertainty interval. The 2021 estimate is used as
    a pragmatic benchmark for the model's 2025 output.

(5) Per-bacteria infection incidence targets sourced primarily from: Antimicrobial
    Resistance Collaborators (2022, Lancet 399:629-655, GRAM study) for major
    pathogens (E. coli, S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, K. pneumoniae, P. aeruginosa,
    A. baumannii, E. faecium, E. faecalis); WHO 2024 STI estimates for N.
    gonorrhoeae (~82M/yr), C. trachomatis (~129M/yr), T. pallidum (~8M/yr);
    WHO FERG 2021-2025 (Majowicz et al. 2026, Lancet Global Health,
    doi:10.1016/j.langlo.2026.103997) for Shigella (~426M), Campylobacter
    (~291M), and ETEC (~260M, used as a conservative floor for the model's
    broader E. coli category); earlier WHO FERG evidence remains relevant to
    non-typhoidal Salmonella and other foodborne targets;
    WHO Global TB Report 2024 for MDR-TB (~400-500K/yr). Smaller healthcare-
    associated pathogens (Citrobacter, Serratia, Stenotrophomonas, Morganella,
    Providencia, B. cepacia) use placeholder estimates extrapolated from regional
    nosocomial surveillance data with greater uncertainty.

(6) Per-bacteria carriage targets sourced from: Human Microbiome Project (HMP,
    NIH 2012) for core gut commensals (E. coli ~95%, B. fragilis ~85%,
    E. faecalis ~80%, S. epidermidis ~95%); Wertheim et al. (2005, Lancet Infect
    Dis 5:751-762) for S. aureus nasal carriage (~20-30%); Bogaert et al. (2004,
    Lancet Infect Dis 4:144-154) for S. pneumoniae nasopharyngeal carriage
    (~35% population-weighted average); CDC GBS screening guidelines for S.
    agalactiae (~25% vaginal/rectal colonization). K. pneumoniae gut carriage
    (20%) from Gorrie et al. (2017, PNAS 114:7655-7660) and regional point-
    prevalence surveys. H. pylori and L. pneumophila set to zero carriage by
    model design (infection-only pathway, no microbiome colonization).

(7) Per-bacteria mortality targets use the GBD 2019 33-pathogen central
    estimates and published 95% uncertainty intervals where definitions align.
    Broader GBD categories are allocated or used as proxies where model
    taxonomies differ; organisms outside that study retain explicitly labelled
    review-informed estimates. Enterobacter spp is divided between the model's
    non-cloacae and separately modelled E. cloacae rows using their previous
    7:4 target ratio. Bacterium-specific model death counters are non-additive
    in polymicrobial deaths and should not be summed to reconstruct the
    person-level headline. H. pylori and MDR-TB remain visible in the organism
    breakdown but are excluded from the 7.7 million headline comparison.

(8) Drug class share targets derived from multiple surveillance sources. ECDC
    Simulation shares use total active antibiotic drug-days across the configured
    drug classes as the denominator, so simulation class shares are compositional
    and sum to 100% apart from rounding.
    ESAC-Net (European Surveillance of Antimicrobial Consumption, annual reports,
    esac-net.europa.eu) provides class-level DDD/1000/day breakdowns for 30 EU/EEA
    countries. Klein et al. (2018, PNAS 115:E3463-E3470) provided global class-level
    consumption from IQVIA pharmaceutical sales data across 76 countries. WHO AWaRe
    classification reports (2019-2023) confirm Access-group antibiotics (penicillins,
    beta-lactam combinations, older cephalosporins, sulfonamides, nitrofurans,
    tetracyclines) account for ~60% of global consumption, Watch-group drugs
    (fluoroquinolones, macrolides, 3G cephalosporins) ~30%, and Reserve drugs <1%.
    Van Boeckel et al. (2014, Lancet Infect Dis 14:742-750) provided additional
    global class breakdowns. Historical targets (2000, 1975, 1950) are interpolated
    from class introduction dates and early adoption curves.

(9) Microbiome resistance simulation output (not calibrated). The simulation
    tracks whether each individual carries ANY resistant mechanism in their
    microbiome for each bacteria/drug combination. No reliable external targets
    exist for this "any resistance" definition: surveillance data measures
    resistance of cultured clinical isolates (dominant strain), while the
    simulation counts any mechanism present. Forslund et al. (2013, Nature
    Commun 4:2151) found resistance genes in virtually all human gut
    metagenomes, suggesting the true "any resistance" proportion is 80-100%.
    These values are presented for information only and are excluded from the
    calibration score.

(10) Resistance-prevalence values are evidence-informed calibration benchmarks,
     not a matrix of direct observed cell estimates. WHO GLASS, ECDC EARS-Net,
     CDC reports, GRAM and organism-specific literature informed the legacy
     bacterium-level notes, but cell-level citations, reference years, specimen
     definitions, denominators and transformations were not retained. The current
     v1 provenance class therefore records that cell provenance is unrecovered;
     it does not label these values as global surveillance medians. Conditional
     mean-any_r values are expert-informed model placeholders, with five explicitly
     identified rare-positive structural priors. The per-row provenance, source and
     rationale identifiers link to data/resistance_target_sources_v1.csv. Evidence-
     quality weights remain unassigned and are not used in scoring. A missing
     benchmark means no comparison value was assigned, not intrinsic resistance.

(11) Some pair-specific resistance targets may not be exactly reproducible under
     the current model structure, especially where data suggest differences between
     closely related drugs that share the same modeled mechanism pathways. These
     residual mismatches are accepted unless sustained evidence supports adding a
     corresponding mechanistic distinction to the model.

(12) Mechanism applicability is no longer duplicated in this summary table. The
     authoritative bacteria/drug/mechanism logic is defined in src/rules/mod.rs
     via mechanism_applies_to_drug(...).
